candidates.name: Angelino Heights / Carroll Avenue and the Echo Park side streets
candidates.reasoning: LA's densest surviving cluster of 19th-century houses inside the urban core, walked for pleasure rather than errands, with the same quiet-pocket-inside-a-loud-city quality Yanaka has and the same slow creep of newcomers restoring old buildings. Nearly as good as South Pasadena and better on the 'preserved neighborhood in the middle of the metropolis' axis; weaker because it lacks Yanaka Ginza's living shopping street of small food stalls.

candidates.name: Little Tokyo (Higashi Honganji, Fugetsu-Do, Nishi Hongwanji, Evergreen Cemetery nearby)
candidates.reasoning: The one LA district where temples, a century-old confectioner, and small family shops sit on the same walkable blocks, giving the temple-and-old-shop texture that defines Yanaka more literally than anywhere else. Docked because it carries a tourist and nightlife layer Yanaka doesn't, and Boyle Heights' Evergreen Cemetery does the everyday-quiet-among-graves role separately rather than in the same fabric.

candidates.name: Micro Center Tustin
candidates.reasoning: Yodobashi Akiba's real role is the pilgrimage megastore: floors of electronics deep enough that hobbyists plan a whole afternoon around it, staff who speak the language of components, and a loyalty-points habit. LA lost that role when Fry's Burbank/City of Industry closed, and Micro Center is the only place people now drive across the basin (and out to Orange County) to browse rather than order online. It's smaller and less of an all-in-one — no cameras, appliances, toys, or watch floor — so the fit is partial, and the drive is a real downgrade from a subway-stop destination.

candidates.name: Samy's Camera
candidates.reasoning: Matches the other half of Yodobashi: the counter where you go because the person behind it actually shoots, knows the body-versus-lens tradeoff, and will let you handle everything, so pros and enthusiasts buy in person at a price they accept instead of clicking. Long-running, LA-identified, and treated as the default answer for camera and video gear in a film town. Narrower than Yodobashi's everything-under-one-roof scale, which is the only reason it isn't first.

candidates.name: Guitar Center Hollywood
candidates.reasoning: The flagship-on-Sunset version of the same idea in the category LA is obsessive about: an oversized store people visit as a destination and a place to loiter in, with staff who play and a wall of gear you're expected to try. Shares Yodobashi's density-as-spectacle feel more than any camera shop does, but it's a national chain with a category-specific audience, so it captures the mood rather than the errand.

source.name: Yona Yona Beer Works
aliases: よなよなビアワークス

candidates.name: Golden Road Brewing
candidates.reasoning: Both are the accessible, big-volume craft brand whose cans are the shorthand for local beer in shops far from home, paired with sprawling pub-style taprooms that serve real food and absorb after-work groups rather than beer-nerd pilgrims. Both also sit under a macro-brewer's ownership (Kirin for Yo-Ho, AB InBev for Golden Road) without losing their hometown-brand affection. The Atwater Village flagship plays the same role as the Akasaka/Aoyama Beer Works: a default weekday-evening meeting point where the beer is good enough and the table is big enough.

candidates.name: Angel City Brewery
candidates.reasoning: Nearly as good a fit for the taproom-as-gathering-place half of the role: a cavernous Arts District hall where downtown workers land after 6pm, with food, long tables, and zero pretension. It loses a little ground on the other half — its cans don't travel or signal 'LA' in out-of-town bottle shops the way Yona Yona's do in Japanese konbini.

candidates.name: Highland Park Brewery
candidates.reasoning: The choice if you weight brewing reputation over reach — it's the LA brewery whose beer people actually argue about, with a taproom that functions as a neighborhood living room. But it's a scene destination rather than the ubiquitous everyday can Yona Yona is, so it fills the craft-flagship role more narrowly.

candidates.name: Original Tommy's (Beverly & Rampart)
candidates.reasoning: Like Yoshinoya, it's one dish executed identically forever — the chili burger instead of the beef bowl — sold cheap, fast, standing or at a counter, 24 hours a day. Neither place is about the room or the company: it's solo fuel for shift workers, cab drivers, and people who need something hot at 3am, and Angelenos defend it with the same shrug-and-loyalty Tokyoites give gyudon.

candidates.name: King Taco
candidates.reasoning: The closest structural match: a homegrown chain dense enough that there's always one nearby, priced so low that eating there is never a decision, open late, and trusted for exactly one thing done consistently. It's the working-class default meal of LA the way gyudon is Tokyo's — nearly as strong an answer as Tommy's, and better on ubiquity, slightly weaker on the 24-hour counter-seat ritual.

candidates.name: Zankou Chicken
candidates.reasoning: A local chain built on a single plate — rotisserie chicken with garlic paste — that people order without looking at the menu, fast and cheap enough for a weekday lunch alone. Less of a late-night hangover institution and a notch pricier than a beef bowl, so it captures the single-dish reliability but not the all-hours function.

candidates.name: Echo Park Lake
candidates.reasoning: Yoyogi's real function is a free, unfenced, walk-in green space pressed right against a youth-culture neighborhood, where the weekend crowd itself is the attraction — drum circles, dance crews, picnic blankets, amateur performers, and a festival calendar. Echo Park Lake plays that role in LA: you walk to it from Sunset, the paddle boats and Lotus Festival draw the whole east side, and the people-watching is the point rather than the scenery. Scale is much smaller, which is the main gap.

candidates.name: Griffith Park
candidates.reasoning: This is the park that appears in every establishing shot and anchors weekly running and hiking rituals, and its Greek Theatre bookings are part of the civic story — closest to Yoyogi's status as the city's default big green space. Nearly as good an answer as Echo Park Lake, and arguably better on scale and civic weight, but it's a car-access wilderness park rather than a station-adjacent lawn where you stumble into rockabilly dancers.

candidates.name: Venice Beach Boardwalk
candidates.reasoning: Captures the specific Yoyogi quality that parks rarely do: free public ground that subcultures colonize as a stage — street performers, muscle beach regulars, costume and dance crews doing their thing weekly with no permit or apparatus. Ranked third only because Venice has hardened into something locals cede to tourists, while Yoyogi remains genuinely residents' territory.

candidates.name: The Broad
candidates.reasoning: Both are the museum where the art is an experience you queue and time-slot for rather than quietly contemplate — the Infinity Mirrored Room reservation scramble is LA's version of the Borderless ticket drop, and both are the default 'art outing' for visitors and young locals who arrive with a photo in mind. Locals grumble about the crowds and the phone-holding while still going and still taking friends from out of town.

candidates.name: Wisdome LA
candidates.reasoning: Closer on medium than on stature: projection-mapped geodesic domes in the Arts District doing full-room immersive digital art, ticketed by time slot, built entirely around being inside the artwork. It lacks The Broad's civic weight and permanent-collection legitimacy, which is exactly what makes it a purer teamLab analogue for anyone who wants the sensation rather than the institution.

candidates.name: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
candidates.reasoning: The newest big-ticket, architecturally showy museum that both tourists and locals treat as a must-do, with timed entry and a spectacle-first approach to its subject. Weaker match because the experience is exhibits and screens about an industry rather than walk-through sensory art — it shares the 'new landmark everyone photographs' role but not the immersive one.
